task_title: Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb
area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain and demonstrate from the right seat a short-field takeoff and maximum performance climb to VX ±5 knots and VY ±5 knots, run a chart-based go/no-go decision with a learner, set up a safe simulated obstacle, and spot and fix the short-field errors learners make most.
why: Short fields and obstacles take away the margin a normal takeoff gives you: the airplane must work at the limit of its takeoff performance, with precise control of attitude and airspeed [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Most stall/spin accidents happen during takeoff and landing, and clearing obstacles on the climb is one of the distractions named as a setup for them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Your learner's first real short strip will be flown without you, so the numbers, the decision and the habits have to come from your lessons.

warmup: Think first: your learner flies a beautiful short-field takeoff from a 5,000-foot runway, VX nailed to the knot, over an 'obstacle' that was never named. Next month they plan to take two friends out of a 2,200-foot grass strip with trees at the end. What did your lesson actually teach them, and what did it leave out?

key_terms.def: A takeoff at the maximum limit of the airplane's takeoff performance, for a short takeoff area or one restricted by obstructions, aiming for the shortest ground roll and steepest climb [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].
The speed that gives the greatest altitude gain for a given distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The speed that gives the greatest altitude gain per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The steepest flight path, flown at VX. In a propeller airplane it comes at a speed below L/DMAX, often just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].
Altitude gained per 100 feet of horizontal travel, as a percentage; 1.5 feet per 100 feet is 1.5 percent [[24:251|AFH 13-2]].
The manufacturer's recommended speed over a 50-foot obstacle. The sample short-field table lists it as the 'AT 50 ft' speed, 56 KIAS at 2,400 pounds [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].
Better performance close to the ground, normally up to one wingspan high, from reduced induced drag [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Holding the airplane on the runway with forward elevator pressure, which overloads the nosewheel and hurts acceleration [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
A point on the runway, chosen before takeoff, where the airplane should be airborne; if it is not, the takeoff is stopped at once [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
The maximum distances available and suitable for takeoff and landing performance; they can be more or less than the runway's physical length [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]].
The difference between pilot capabilities and the task requirements of the flight. Accidents often happen when requirements exceed capability [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].
An obstacle the instructor names at a realistic point so a learner can practice an obstacle-clearance takeoff without a real one [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

chunks.title: The maneuver and the standard you hold

body.p: Purpose: when the takeoff area is short, or obstructions restrict it, you fly the airplane at the limit of its takeoff performance to get the shortest ground roll and the steepest climb [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. The power, flap setting, airspeeds and procedure come from the performance section of the POH/AFM [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. The normal takeoff skills (rudder, tracking, lift-off attitude) are taught in the Normal Takeoff and Climb lesson (AI.VII.A); this lesson builds on them.

Procedure in one breath: start at the very beginning of the takeoff area with flaps set, apply full power smoothly, roll in a low-drag attitude, rotate as VX approaches, climb at VX until the obstacle is cleared or at least 50 feet, then lower the nose slightly to VY and climb to a safe maneuvering altitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]] [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

body.p: The Commercial ACS already holds the obstacle speed and VY to ±5 knots (ACS CA.IV.E.S10, S11, S13), so a commercial applicant who becomes your learner is held to your window. Your Area VII test will include at least two takeoff and two landing Tasks chosen by the evaluator (ACS Area VII Note).

callout.text: In some airplanes a 5-knot error costs a lot of climb, so precise airspeed control is the point of the maneuver, not a checkride detail [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Say that to the learner on the ground, before the first try.

check.q: Your learner's POH obstacle clearance speed is 59 KIAS. They cross a simulated obstacle at 68 KIAS. Did they meet their private standard, and would that pass for you?
check.a: Private: yes, the window is 54 to 69 knots (+10/-5, ACS PA.IV.E.S10). You: no, your window is 54 to 64 knots (±5, ACS AI.VII.E.S10).

chunks.title: VX, VY and why the angle matters here

body.p: Best angle of climb speed (VX): most altitude for the distance over the ground. Best rate of climb speed (VY): most altitude for the time. VX is usually a little slower than VY, and both come from the POH/AFM [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. VX is the tool for a short field surrounded by trees or power lines: clear the obstacle while covering the least ground [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

The PHAK example makes the trade concrete: on its maximum angle profile an airplane reaches 1,000 feet AGL in 30 seconds but covers only 3,000 feet over the ground; on its maximum rate profile it climbs to 1,500 feet in the same 30 seconds but covers 6,000 feet [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Both use maximum throttle; the difference is the airspeed and angle of attack [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

bullets: Where VX sits: in a propeller airplane, maximum excess thrust (maximum angle) normally comes below L/DMAX and often just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]. Teach your learner that VX is a slow, high angle of attack speed with little margin.

What changes it: more weight, more altitude, gear down or flaps down all reduce excess thrust and power, so both maximum angle and maximum rate get worse [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. As altitude goes up, VX increases and VY decreases until they meet at the absolute ceiling [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

Ground effect: lift-off and the first part of the climb happen within about one wingspan of the surface. At a height of 1/10 span induced drag is about 50 percent lower, at 1/4 span about 25 percent lower [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Climbing out, the airplane needs more angle of attack and more thrust [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

callout.text: In ground effect the airplane may seem able to fly below the recommended speed, but climbing out below it gives much less climb than VY or even VX. At high density altitude, high temperature or maximum weight it may lift off and then be unable to climb out of ground effect or clear obstructions [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

check.q: A learner asks, 'If VX is the steepest climb, why not just use it all the way to pattern altitude?' What do you say?
check.a: VX buys angle, not time: VY gives the most altitude per minute [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Once the obstacle is cleared or you are at least 50 feet up, lower the nose slightly and climb at VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

chunks.title: Air, weight, wind and the takeoff surface

body.p: Density altitude: thin air means less engine power, less propeller thrust and less lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. At altitude the airplane lifts off at the same indicated airspeed as at sea level, but at a higher true airspeed, and an unsupercharged engine loses power right away [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. The most critical takeoffs combine high weight, altitude, temperature and unfavorable wind [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

body.p: Landing surface/condition: chart numbers assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway. Grass, gravel, dirt, ruts, mud, snow and standing water all slow acceleration [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. An upslope lengthens the ground run and a downslope shortens it; surface and slope are listed in the Chart Supplement [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. A wet runway also hurts the abort, because hydroplaning tires give almost no braking or steering [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Soft surfaces call for the soft-field technique, which is quite different from the short-field technique on a firm, smooth surface [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

Charts come as tables, graphs or combined graphs [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. The combined graph above handles temperature, pressure altitude, weight, wind and obstacle height on one sheet. Its worked example (2,000 feet, 22 °C, 2,600 pounds, 6-knot headwind, 50-foot obstacle) gives a 700-foot ground roll and 1,400 feet total, with lift-off at 63 knots and 68 knots over the obstacle [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]] [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]]. Note its conditions box: flaps up. It is not a short-field chart.

callout.text: On a combined graph a small error at the start becomes a large error at the end [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. Have the learner trace it with a straightedge while you watch, and check the answer against common sense.

check.q: Your learner reads a combined takeoff graph quickly and gets 1,100 feet over 50 feet for a hot, heavy day. The table version for a similar airplane says 2,000. What do you teach?
check.a: A small reading error early on a combined graph grows into a large error at the end, so read it slowly and accurately [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. Hot and heavy should lengthen the distance, not shorten it [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

chunks.title: Choosing the runway: chart-based go/no-go with a learner

callout.text: Before every flight the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data from the approved flight manual, or other reliable data for elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Airplane performance and limitations: work the short-field chart together. Find the weight, then the pressure altitude row, then the temperature column; read ground roll and total to clear 50 feet; then apply the notes [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]]. The PHAK's own example at 2,400 pounds, 3,000 feet, 30 °C and an 18-knot headwind ends at 1,060 feet of ground roll and 1,984 feet total [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]].

bullets: Read the conditions box first: flaps 10°, full throttle prior to brake release, paved level runway, zero wind [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

Read the notes: lean for maximum rpm above 3,000 feet elevation; minus 10 percent per 9 knots of headwind; plus 10 percent per 2 knots of tailwind up to 10 knots; dry grass adds 15 percent of the ground roll figure [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].
Chart data come from a new airplane flown with average skill. Adjust for a worn airplane or below-average technique [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].
When you interpolate, rounding toward the more adverse value gives a small safety margin [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

body.p: Available distance: declared distances can be more or less than the painted runway [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]]. If ATC offers an intersection and you want the full length, you are expected to say so [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10]]. Takeoff plus landing ground roll from the POH is a good estimate of the runway needed to accelerate and then stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Wind: at a towered field with wind of 5 knots or more, ATC assigns the runway most nearly aligned with it, and tailwind and crosswind considerations come before noise abatement. Ask for another runway if you need it [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]].

Pilot capability: the chart describes the airplane, not your learner. The RMH comfort-level table has a 'shortest runway' box, and a pilot who has never used a runway shorter than 5,000 feet should write 5,000 there [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. The RMH suggests adjusting personal minimums for special conditions such as an unfamiliar airport, for example adding at least 500 feet to runway length [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Margin of safety is pilot capability minus task requirements, and it shrinks in critical phases [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

A worked go/no-go from the RMH: at 6,700 feet pressure altitude and 25 °C, the pilot's airplane needs 4,700 feet over 50 feet at 2,740 pounds, or 3,600 feet at 2,500 pounds [[30:32|RMH 3-14]]. With her 20 percent margin, 4,700 feet becomes 5,640 feet, more than the 5,000-foot runway [[30:36|RMH 4-3]]. She sends her passengers by taxi to a 9,200-foot runway and picks them up there [[30:41|RMH 5-3]].

callout.text: Teaching tip: make the learner say the decision and the margin out loud ('Chart says 1,500, plus my margin is 1,800, runway is 2,400: go'). Factoring performance data to create safety margins is an RMH risk mitigation [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

check.q: Using Figure 11-24: 2,200 pounds, 6,000 feet pressure altitude, 10 °C, zero wind. What total distance does the learner need to clear 50 feet, and what does the table say they lift off at?
check.a: 2,355 feet total, with lift-off at 49 KIAS and 54 KIAS at 50 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

chunks.title: Configuration: flaps, trim, mixture and gear

bullets: Flaps: if the manufacturer recommends flaps, set them before the roll so all your attention goes to technique and performance [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. POH flap guidance for takeoff is based on climb performance; never exceed it [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
Trim: failure to have the airplane properly trimmed prior to takeoff is a listed short-field error [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
Mixture: above 3,000 feet elevation, the sample chart wants the mixture leaned for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].
Propeller: for maximum takeoff power the propeller control goes full forward (low pitch, high rpm) [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

Gear and flaps after lift-off: keep them in takeoff position until clear of obstacles (or as the manufacturer says) and VY is established. At a stable VY, retract the gear and then the flaps, usually in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift and settling. Then set normal climb power [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

body.p: Never retract the gear before the instruments show a positive rate of climb, especially after a premature lift-off, and plan the gear-up point for runway length, climb gradient, obstacles and terrain [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]. In some airplanes, delaying gear retraction after a short-runway takeoff may be worth it, so the gear can absorb energy in an off-airport landing [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

callout.text: Leaning forward to reach the gear selector can put forward pressure on the yoke and make the airplane descend [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]. Until all obstacles are cleared, the AFH wants the pilot looking outside, not reaching for controls [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

check.q: Climbing at a stable VY after the obstacle, your learner moves the flaps from 10° to 0° in one motion and the airplane sinks. What should they have done?
check.a: Raise the flaps in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift and settling [[24:144|AFH 6-12]], and only after VY is established and obstacles are cleared.

chunks.title: Before the roll: checklists, radios, runway, wind and all the runway

body.p: These steps are the same as a normal takeoff (see AI.VII.A). What changes for a short field is where the airplane starts and what the learner must have settled before the roll.

bullets: Checklists: complete the before-takeoff checklist, including the flap setting and, at high fields, the leaned mixture [[24:143|AFH 6-11]] [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Model doing the items, then confirming with the checklist [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

Radio calls: at a nontowered field, say the airport name at the start and end of each call and never say 'active runway' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. If you need full length or a different runway, tell ATC [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]].
Verify the runway: set the heading bug to the runway heading and confirm they agree before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
Wind: the large end of a wind cone points into the wind; don't use a tetrahedron for wind direction [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]]. Without an indicator, read smoke, dust, trees or water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Controls for wind while taxiing: quartering headwind, upwind aileron up; quartering tailwind, elevator down and upwind aileron down [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Start a crosswind roll with full aileron into the wind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

Clear and align using all the runway: clear the approach and takeoff paths, then start from the very beginning of the takeoff area, aligned with the takeoff path [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Failure to use all available runway is a listed error [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

callout.text: Make the learner back-taxi or turn tight onto the threshold on a short runway and point to the first usable foot. A learner who starts 300 feet down a 2,000-foot strip has given away 15 percent of the runway before the throttle moves.

check.q: The tower offers your learner an intersection departure on a runway that is just long enough from the end. What should the learner say?
check.a: Ask for full length. If for any reason a pilot prefers the full length, the pilot is expected to tell ATC [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10]].

chunks.title: Fly it and explain it from the right seat

body.p: On the checkride you fly and talk at once. Each step below has what you do and a short line you can say.

head: Step
What you do
What you say
rows: Brakes and power
Hold the brakes and set full power, as the ACS asks and the chart assumes (full throttle prior to brake release) (ACS AI.VII.E.S7) [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]
'Brakes firm, full power, feet ready.'
Confirm before release
Check rpm and engine gauges at full power before releasing; check flight instruments before rotation (ACS AI.VII.E.S8) [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
'Full power, rpm where the POH says, gauges green. Brakes off.'
Roll
Full weight on the mains, low-drag attitude; a nosewheel airplane needs little elevator [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Rudder for the centerline, aileron into any crosswind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]
'Nose down, low drag, let it accelerate.'
Rotate
As VX approaches, back pressure to the VX attitude for a smooth, firm lift-off [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
'Coming up on VX: rotate to this picture.'
Hold VX
More back pressure as it accelerates to hold a constant speed; wings level; VX until the obstacle is cleared or at least 50 feet [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
'VX, wings level, eyes outside until we are past the trees.'
Transition
Lower the pitch slightly and climb at VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
'Fifty feet, obstacle clear: nose down a little to VY.'
Clean up
At a stable VY with a positive rate, gear up, flaps up in increments, then climb power [[24:144|AFH 6-12]] [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
'Positive rate, VY stable: gear up, flaps up in steps.'
Climb out
VY to a safe maneuvering altitude, crab on the extended centerline [[24:144|AFH 6-12]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]
'Holding VY, crabbing to stay on centerline.'

body.p: Some airplanes want to fly well before VX. Then let it lift off in ground effect, lower the pitch to level and accelerate to VX with the wheels just clear of the runway. That is better than holding it on with forward pressure, which loads the nosewheel, can cause wheelbarrowing and hurts acceleration [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

Directional control and wind drift: keep the nose straight with rudder on the roll, then crab into the wind after lift-off to track the extended centerline [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]. Noise abatement: procedures come from the Chart Supplement, local publications and the tower; ask the tower if unsure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Tailwind and crosswind still come first [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]].

callout.text: Every foot, full power, low drag, VX at 50, VY to clean up.

check.q: Right after lift-off at VX the airplane accelerates and your learner holds the same pitch. What happens to the airspeed, and what should they do?
check.a: It climbs past VX, because the airplane accelerates more rapidly after lift-off. They need additional back pressure to hold a constant airspeed [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

chunks.title: Wind, windshear and wake at low speed and high pitch

head: Effect
On a short-field takeoff
What you teach
rows: Crosswind
The controls are deflected for the whole roll, which adds drag and costs early performance [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. A rising upwind wing can lead to side-skipping [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]

Full aileron into the wind at brake release, less as speed builds; after lift-off, crab on the extended centerline [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]. Check the crosswind against the demonstrated value, about 0.2 VSO or the placard [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]
Windshear
A headwind turning to a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the roll the only sign may be slow airspeed build-up, and gusts can hide it [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]
Recovery needs holding or increasing pitch and accepting lower airspeed, the opposite of what airspeed-precision training teaches [[28:267|AWH 22-12]]. Near convective weather, wait it out
Tailwind
A tailwind of 10 percent of takeoff speed adds about 21 percent to takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. The sample chart adds 10 percent for every 2 knots, up to 10 knots [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]
Use the POH correction, and remember the AIM puts tailwind ahead of noise abatement in runway choice [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]]
Wake turbulence
Vortices start at the larger aircraft's rotation [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. Short-span trainers have a harder time countering the roll [[34:148|AIM 7-4-3]]
Rotate before its rotation point and climb above its path until clear; be alert for any critical takeoff situation that could lead to a vortex encounter [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]

body.p: A tailwind also hurts the climb over the trees: unlike rate of climb, climb gradient is affected by wind; a headwind component improves it and a tailwind component reduces it [[24:259|AFH 13-10]]. Application: at VX the airplane is slow, often just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]], so a sudden airspeed loss from a gust, shear or vortex leaves less margin than at VY.

callout.text: The AFH normal-takeoff advice for strong, gusty winds is extra speed before lift-off [[24:137|AFH 6-5]], but extra speed lengthens the takeoff distance with the square of speed [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. On a short field in gusts, that conflict is a reason to question the takeoff, not to split the difference.

check.q: A light business jet just rotated about a third of the way down your runway. Your learner is ready for a short-field takeoff from the threshold. What plan do you brief?
check.a: Note its rotation point, rotate before it, and climb above its climb path until turning clear of its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Vortices begin at rotation [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

chunks.title: Rejected takeoff and engine failure in the VX climb

body.p: Rejected takeoff: plan for it before the roll. Pick the point on the runway where the airplane should be airborne; if you get there and are not flying, stop right away [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Reasons include a powerplant problem, poor acceleration, a runway incursion or a traffic conflict. To reject: throttle to idle, maximum braking, keep directional control; for a fire, mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off; always the manufacturer's procedure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

On a short runway the abort point is close to the start and the remaining runway is short. Use the estimate of takeoff plus landing ground roll to see whether a stop is even possible past that point [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Check the engine instruments for signs of a malfunction after applying power [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]; a malfunctioning powerplant or poor acceleration is a reason to reject the takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Setting power against the brakes lets the learner make that check before the airplane moves (ACS AI.VII.E.S8).

Potential engine failure in takeoff/climb phase: at a climb pitch without power the airplane is at or near a stalling angle of attack, and the pilot may still be holding right rudder. Lower the nose at once, center the rudder, and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. A VX climb has a higher pitch and a lower speed than a VY climb, so the nose has further to go and there is less time (application, from [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]).

Turning back: the AFH example from 300 feet AGL ends 1,016 feet below the runway, and a turn back is an unacceptable risk for student, low-time and unproficient pilots [[24:356|AFH 18-7]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

Low altitude maneuvering, stall, spin and CFIT: trying to pull the airplane off early or climb too steeply can settle it back onto the runway or into the obstacles [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Power-on stalls are practiced in the takeoff configuration so pilots recognize an accidental stall while trying to clear an obstacle [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. CFIT often follows flight at high density altitude or in mountainous terrain [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]: compare the chart climb with the terrain past the runway.

callout.text: In the RMH case of a near-gross-weight takeoff from a 3,100-foot wet turf strip toward 100-foot trees, the stall warning sounded just before the airplane hit the trees. The POH had no data for wet grass or a 100-foot obstacle [[30:64|RMH C-1]].

check.q: Your learner briefs, 'If the engine quits at 150 feet over the trees, I'll hold VX to clear them.' What is wrong with that plan?
check.a: At climb pitch without power the airplane is at or near the stall angle of attack. The first action is to lower the nose, center the rudder and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

chunks.title: Traffic, distractions and staying ahead of the airplane

body.p: Collision hazards: in one study of midair collisions a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the accidents, and most happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. In a steep VX climb the nose hides traffic ahead. After the obstacle, adjust pitch to see over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Turn the landing light on when cleared for takeoff, or at the start of the roll at a nontowered field [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

Distractions and task prioritization: preoccupation with configuration or trim, avoiding traffic, or clearing obstacles during takeoff and climb can set up a stall/spin [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Teach the order: fly the VX attitude, clear the obstacle, then touch flaps and gear [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

Loss of situational awareness: the instructor's own talking is a hazard. There may be no time to teach during the takeoff, and anything you say may not be heard; do most of the teaching before calling the tower or announcing on the CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Avoid teaching takeoff technique while entering the runway, when attention belongs on control and a clear runway [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Disorientation: rapid takeoff acceleration can give a false nose-up feeling when visual references are poor, and the pilot may push the nose down [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A night short-field departure over dark trees is exactly that setup; brief it.

callout.text: The intentional practice of stalls seldom causes accidents; inadvertent stalls from distraction do [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Build distraction practice at altitude, not in the first 50 feet over real trees.

check.q: Lined up for a short-field takeoff, your learner asks you to explain once more how to rotate. Why does the AIH say not to start now?
check.a: Teaching while entering the runway pulls attention from control and runway clearance, and during the takeoff it may not be heard. Do most of the teaching before calling the tower or the CTAF call [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

body.p: Most training runways have no 50-foot trees, so you create one. The AIH says to specify where an imaginary obstacle exists, at a realistic point, and warns that the scenario must not lead the learner into an unsafe climb rate or excessive pitch attitude [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The ACS defines the end of the VX segment for a simulated obstacle: 50 feet AGL (ACS AI.VII.E.S10, S11).

bullets: Name it on the ground: 'a 50-foot tree line at the far taxiway sign.' A vague obstacle invites a learner to chase a vague target. (Application of [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].)
Make the transition point clear: at 50 feet, or once past the named obstacle, lower the nose to VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

Watch pitch, not just airspeed: a learner trying hard to 'clear' something may raise the nose past the VX attitude. Too steep a climb can settle the airplane back or into obstacles [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

Simulated engine failures: done wrong they have caused real emergencies and accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Agree beforehand who has the throttle, and end every simulation as soon as the outcome is clear [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: Add realism in layers. The AIH short-field example: once the skill is solid on a 6,000-foot obstruction-free runway, discuss the same airplane on an 1,800-foot strip with an obstruction off the end, near maximum gross weight and at high density altitude [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. The ground discussion costs little and builds the judgment the maneuver exists for.

callout.text: No single-engine source gives a minimum altitude or method for simulating a power loss in the VX climb. Treat that as a school SOP and instructor judgment item, not something to improvise over real obstacles.

check.q: You tell your learner, 'Pretend there are trees out there.' They climb at VX to 400 feet. What went wrong in your setup?
check.a: The obstacle was not specified. The AIH says to name where the imaginary obstacle is, at a realistic point [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; without one the ACS endpoint is 50 feet AGL, then VY (ACS AI.VII.E.S10, S11).

bullets: Prerequisite blocks: humans learn from simple to complex, and the AIH example is mastering the normal landing before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]; the same order fits takeoffs. Slow flight and power-on stalls in takeoff configuration feed this lesson [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

Tie it to the course: relate the short-field lesson to both the certification and the safety objectives [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The certification goal is VX ±5; the safety goal is the go/no-go at a real strip.
Ground brief: chart work with the learner, the abort point and its landmark, the engine-failure plan, the named obstacle, and who has the controls [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Demonstrate first on a long runway with a simulated obstacle, explaining each step, then let the learner talk you through it before they fly it (application; see the patter in chunk 7).

Learner's turns: stay quiet on the roll, since teaching during the takeoff may not be heard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Watch the rotation point, pitch at VX, eyes outside until clear, and hands off the flap lever [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
Grow the scenario: when the skill is consistent, add weight, density altitude, a grass surface and a shorter runway on the ground first, then in the air [[25:30|AIH 1-26]] [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

body.p: What makes this Task hard to teach (application): the errors happen fast and look alike. A low, flat climb can be early rotation (high drag), a weak engine, or a learner chasing the airspeed needle. Watch the attitude at rotation and the airspeed trend in the first 5 seconds, and name what you saw before you suggest a fix.

callout.text: A learner's self-assessment after a short-field takeoff should include a number: 'Lift-off about 1,000 feet down; VX within 3 knots; 50 feet before the taxiway sign.' Numbers make the next go/no-go decision real.

check.q: Your learner's normal landings are still inconsistent, and the syllabus says short-field work is next. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Delay the short-field block and review an earlier block, such as slow flight, which lets the learner do well and rebuild skills for normal approaches and landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Normal landings come before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

body.p: The errors below are the AFH list for short-field takeoffs and maximum performance climbs [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. The 'what you see' and 'fix' columns use the AFH text around that list.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to review AFM/POH and performance charts
The learner can't state the expected distance, speeds or abort point
Work the chart together on the ground and set the abort point [[24:143|AFH 6-11]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Failure to adequately clear the area
No look along final or the runway before lining up
Make 'final clear, runway clear' a spoken habit [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]
Failure to utilize all available runway/takeoff area
Lineup well past the threshold
Start at the very beginning of the takeoff area [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]
Failure to have the airplane properly trimmed prior to takeoff
Heavy or wandering pitch after lift-off
Trim on the before-takeoff checklist [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Premature lift-off resulting in high drag
Nose up early, mushy acceleration, flat climb
Hold the low-drag attitude; rotate as VX approaches [[24:143|AFH 6-11]] [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Holding the airplane on the ground with excessive forward pressure
Nosewheel loaded, possible wheelbarrowing
Let it lift off, then level in ground effect to accelerate to VX [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Inadequate rotation resulting in excessive speed after lift-off
Airspeed well above VX through 50 feet, shallow climb
Rotate to the VX attitude and add back pressure as it accelerates [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Inability to attain/maintain VX
Airspeed wanders outside ±5 knots
Fly the attitude, then check airspeed; small corrections [[24:142|AFH 6-10]] [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]
Fixation on the airspeed indicator during initial climb
Head down, pitch oscillating, wings not level
Eyes outside on the attitude until clear; quick airspeed glances [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Premature retraction of landing gear and/or wing flaps
Hand on the flap lever over the obstacle; settling
Keep takeoff configuration until clear and at VY; flaps in increments [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]

body.p: On the checkride the examiner may fly as your learner and make one of these errors. Say what you saw, the likely cause and the fix. When a task needs reteaching, the AIH has the instructor demonstrate it, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Through 50 feet your learner is at 72 KIAS with a VX of 62, every time. Which listed error is it, and what is your fix?
check.a: Inadequate rotation resulting in excessive speed after lift-off [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Rotate to the VX attitude as VX approaches, then add back pressure as the airplane accelerates to hold the speed [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

f1.alt: A high-wing trainer starts at the very beginning of a runway, rotates at approximately VX, climbs steeply at VX over a stand of trees just past the runway end, then climbs at VY, where a note says to retract gear and flaps.

f2.caption: Figure 11-7. Maximum angle of climb (AOC) versus maximum rate of climb (ROC).
f2.alt: Two airplanes start climbing from the same point toward a tall radio tower. The airplane on the steeper Max AOC line is higher at any given distance than the airplane on the flatter Max ROC line.

f3.caption: Figure 6-9. Effect of premature lift-off.
f3.alt: Five airplanes along a runway: premature rotation increases drag, decreases acceleration and increases takeoff distance; the airplane may lift off at low airspeed; flight below VX gives a shallow climb; and the airplane may settle back to the ground.

f4.caption: Figure 11-24. Takeoff distance short field charts.
f4.alt: A short-field takeoff distance table. Conditions: flaps 10 degrees, full throttle prior to brake release, paved level runway, zero wind. Notes: lean for maximum rpm above 3,000 feet elevation; decrease distances 10 percent per 9 knots headwind and increase 10 percent per 2 knots tailwind up to 10 knots; on dry grass add 15 percent of the ground roll. Rows for 2,400, 2,200 and 2,000 pounds with lift-off and 50-foot speeds, from sea level to 8,000 feet pressure altitude, and columns for 0 to 40 degrees C giving ground roll and total distance to clear a 50-foot obstacle.

f5.caption: Figure 11-23. Takeoff distance graph.
f5.alt: A combined takeoff distance graph with four panels read left to right: outside air temperature with pressure altitude lines, weight from 2,800 to 2,200 pounds, wind component with headwind and tailwind guide lines, and obstacle height from 0 to 50 feet, ending on a distance scale from 0 to 6,000 feet. A table gives lift-off and 50-foot speeds by weight, and a box lists the associated conditions: full throttle 2,600 rpm, mixture leaned to appropriate fuel pressure, flaps up, gear retracted after positive climb, cowl flaps open. A red example line is drawn through all four panels.

f6.alt: A ribbon chart of task load over time through preflight, takeoff, cruise, and approach and landing. A pilot capabilities band sits above a task requirements band; the orange space between them is the margin of safety, which narrows during takeoff and nearly disappears during approach and landing.

scenario.title: Two friends, a grass strip and a tree line
scenario.setup: Your private-pilot learner has done well on short-field takeoffs at your home field: 5,000 feet of pavement and an imaginary 50-foot obstacle. Now they want a lesson at a private 2,300-foot turf strip, so they can fly two friends out of it next month. The grass is damp from morning dew, there are 60-foot trees past the far end, field elevation is 3,400 feet, and the afternoon will be hot. A light southerly wind is shifting, and cumulus is building over the hills.

questions.q: What has to be true before this lesson even leaves the ground?
questions.a: The learner must know the POH distance data for elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]] and work the short-field chart, including its notes for leaning and grass [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. The chart assumes a new airplane and average skill [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]], and the obstacle here is taller than the chart's 50 feet.

questions.q: The POH has no data for wet grass or a 60-foot obstacle. How do you use that gap as a teaching point?
questions.a: That was the situation in the RMH turf-strip accident, where the POH had no data for wet grass or a 100-foot obstacle and the airplane hit the trees [[30:64|RMH C-1]]. Teach the learner to treat missing data as added risk that needs mitigation, not as permission [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

questions.q: The learner's plan is the trip with both friends. What mitigation does the RMH case suggest?
questions.a: Fly the airplane solo out of the strip and meet the passengers at a nearby longer airport. In the RMH case that single action addressed both the environment and performance risks and reduced the external pressure [[30:65|RMH C-2]].

questions.q: The wind shifts between a light headwind and a light tailwind. How does that change the go/no-go?
questions.a: A tailwind of 10 percent of takeoff speed adds about 21 percent to distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]], and the sample chart adds 10 percent for each 2 knots [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Plan for the worse wind, and wait or choose the other direction if the numbers no longer fit. Crosswind adds drag from deflected controls [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

questions.q: What do you watch for from the building cumulus?
questions.a: Convective weather can produce windshear and microbursts [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the roll, slow airspeed build-up may be the only sign [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. If the cumulus grows toward the strip, the lesson waits.

questions.q: What do you brief about the abort, an engine failure and the climb over the trees?
questions.a: An abort point with a landmark and power to idle with maximum braking if it is reached on the ground [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]; a wet surface hurts braking [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. If the engine quits in the climb, nose down at once and land ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Eyes outside until the trees are behind, no flap or gear handling [[24:144|AFH 6-12]], and a scan for traffic at a nontowered field [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

skills.do: Complete the before-takeoff and after-takeoff checklists, explaining the short-field items: flaps, trim, mixture for elevation.
skills.practice: Brief the checklist items you add for a short field, then do the flow and confirm with the checklist [[24:36|AFH 1-15]] [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

skills.do: Make the departure radio calls, including asking for full length or another runway when needed.
skills.practice: Script a CTAF call with the airport name at both ends and a tower request for full length [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]] [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10]].

skills.do: Verify the assigned or correct runway before adding power, and explain how.
skills.practice: Heading bug to runway heading; confirm they agree on lineup [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

skills.do: Determine wind direction with or without an indicator and explain what it does to the short-field numbers.
skills.practice: Read the sock and natural signs on every flight, then apply the chart wind note [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

skills.do: Position the flight controls for the wind and explain each position.
skills.practice: Call the control position on taxi and at lineup; full aileron into the wind at brake release [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

skills.do: Clear the area, taxi into position and align on the centerline at the very beginning of the takeoff area, saying why every foot counts.
skills.practice: Practice tight turns onto the threshold; explain the 'use all available runway' error [[24:143|AFH 6-11]] [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

skills.do: Apply brakes while setting engine power to achieve maximum performance, explaining the chart condition behind it.
skills.practice: Hold the brakes, set full power, explain why the chart assumes full throttle prior to brake release [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

skills.do: Confirm takeoff power prior to brake release and verify engine and flight instrument indications prior to rotation, aloud.
skills.practice: Know your airplane's static full-power rpm and call it before releasing the brakes.

skills.do: Rotate and lift off at the recommended airspeed and accelerate to the recommended obstacle clearance airspeed or VX, ±5 knots, while explaining (ACS AI.VII.E.S9).
skills.practice: Rotate as VX approaches to the VX attitude; add back pressure as it accelerates [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

skills.do: Hold the recommended obstacle clearance airspeed or VX, ±5 knots, until the obstacle is cleared or 50 feet above the surface (ACS AI.VII.E.S10).
skills.practice: Fly VX at altitude with a partner calling every 2-knot drift, then over a named imaginary obstacle [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

skills.do: Pitch for VY and accelerate to VY ±5 knots after the obstacle or at 50 feet AGL if simulating (ACS AI.VII.E.S11).
skills.practice: Practice the small pitch-down at 50 feet and say 'VY' before you do it [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane per the manufacturer after a positive rate of climb is verified, explaining the order.
skills.practice: At a stable VY: positive rate, gear up, flaps up in increments, climb power [[24:144|AFH 6-12]] [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

skills.do: Maintain VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude while instructing (ACS AI.VII.E.S13).
skills.practice: Fly the full patter to pattern altitude until the talking costs no airspeed.

skills.do: Maintain directional control and wind-drift correction through the roll and climb.
skills.practice: Rudder for the centerline, aileron into the wind, then crab on the extended centerline [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Comply with noise abatement procedures and explain where they come from and what takes priority.
skills.practice: Look up each airport's procedures; know that tailwind and crosswind come before noise programs [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors, usually a simulated error flown by the examiner as your learner.
skills.practice: For each AFH-listed error, practice saying what you see, the cause and the fix [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what is the objective at rotation on a short-field takeoff?
options: Rotate as soon as the controls feel firm, to get off early
Rotate to the appropriate pitch attitude at or near VX
Rotate at the normal-takeoff lift-off speed from the POH
Rotate at VY so there is a speed margin over the trees
quiz.why: The objective is to rotate to the appropriate pitch attitude at (or near) VX [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

quiz.q: In a propeller airplane, where does the PHAK say maximum excess thrust, and so the maximum angle of climb, normally occurs?
options: Above L/DMAX, close to the normal cruise climb speed
Exactly at L/DMAX, the same speed as best glide
Below L/DMAX, frequently just above stall speed
At VY, where excess power is greatest
quiz.why: In a propeller airplane maximum excess thrust normally occurs below L/DMAX and frequently just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH suggest raising flaps in increments after a short-field climb?
options: To meet airport noise abatement climb profiles
To keep the stall warning horn from sounding on climb-out
To avoid a sudden loss of lift and settling
To limit loads on the flap motor and tracks
quiz.why: It is usually advisable to raise the flaps in increments to avoid sudden loss of lift and settling [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

quiz.q: The AIH uses short-field takeoffs and landings as its example of tying a lesson to the course. What should that lesson be related to?
options: Only the certification objectives listed in the practical test ACS
The learner's personal flying goals for after the checkride
The performance section of the airplane's POH alone
Both the certification and the safety objectives of the course
quiz.why: A lesson on short-field takeoffs and landings should be related to both the certification and safety objectives of the course of training [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

quiz.q: Which item is on the AFH list of short-field takeoff common errors?
options: Insufficient back-elevator pressure during the initial takeoff roll
Mechanical use of aileron control instead of judging position
Not leveling off low enough to stay in ground effect
Failure to have the airplane properly trimmed prior to takeoff
quiz.why: Trim is on the short-field list [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. The others come from the soft-field and crosswind lists [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: On the sample short-field table, what does note 1 tell a pilot departing a 4,500-foot elevation airport?
options: Use flaps 20 instead of flaps 10 above that elevation
Add 15 percent of the ground roll to both distances
Lean for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup
Decrease all distances 10 percent for the thinner air
quiz.why: Above 3,000 feet elevation, lean to give maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

quiz.q: In the RMH comfort-level table, what should a pilot write for 'shortest runway' if they have never used a runway shorter than 5,000 feet?
options: 2,500 feet, the sample single-engine value
The POH total distance over a 50-foot obstacle
Whatever length the airplane's chart says it can use
5,000 feet, the shortest they have actually used
quiz.why: If the pilot has never operated from a runway shorter than 5,000 feet, the box should say 5,000 feet [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].

quiz.q: The AIH wants realistic takeoff scenarios. What must a takeoff scenario NOT lead the learner into?
options: Any obstacle the learner cannot actually see from the runway
A takeoff from a runway longer than the strip being simulated
An unsafe climb rate or an excessive pitch attitude
A decision the learner has to make before the takeoff roll
quiz.why: The scenario should not create hazards that result in the learner attempting to maintain an unsafe climb rate or excessive pitch attitude [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

quiz.q: Ground effect makes the airspeed indicator and altimeter read how, and why does that matter at lift-off?
options: Slightly high, because the static source sees lower pressure
Slightly low, from higher static pressure near the ground
Erratically, until the airplane climbs out of it
Correctly, because ground effect changes only induced drag
quiz.why: Ground effect raises local static pressure, so airspeed and altitude read slightly low; climbing out, indicated airspeed increases [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: Your learner's airplane wants to fly well before VX on every short-field roll. What does the AFH recommend?
options: Let it lift off, then level off in ground effect to accelerate to VX
Hold it on the runway with firm forward pressure until reaching VX
Climb right away at whatever speed it lifts off to clear the trees
Raise the flaps during the roll so it stays on the runway longer
quiz.why: Let it lift off in ground effect and reduce pitch to level until it accelerates to VX with the wheels just clear; holding it on with forward pressure loads the nosewheel and can cause wheelbarrowing [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner holds the brakes, sets full power and asks if this always shortens the roll. Best answer?
options: Not proven for all singles, but use the POH method: this chart assumes it
No; release the brakes first and then add power smoothly every time
Yes; the AFH says it shortens the takeoff roll in every light single-engine airplane
It matters only for turbocharged engines, which need time to spool
final_quiz.why: The AFH says it has not been established in all light singles [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]; the sample chart condition is full throttle prior to brake release [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]], and the ACS asks for brakes while setting power (ACS AI.VII.E.S7).

final_quiz.q: Simulating an obstacle, your learner lowers the nose to VY at 30 feet because 'we're clear.' What standard did they miss?
options: No standard; any height works when the obstacle is only simulated
Hold the obstacle clearance speed or VX until 50 feet AGL
Hold VX until passing over the departure end of the runway
Hold VX until reaching 500 feet AGL, then accelerate to VY
final_quiz.why: With no obstacle, climb at VX to at least 50 feet before lowering the pitch to VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]; the ACS endpoint is 50 feet AGL if simulating (ACS AI.VII.E.S10, S11).

final_quiz.q: Every rotation, your learner's nose comes up about 10 knots before VX and the airplane accelerates slowly in a mushy, nose-high roll. Which AFH error, and fix?
options: Airspeed fixation; look outside and ignore the airspeed indicator entirely
Excess forward pressure; add back pressure earlier in the roll
Premature lift-off with high drag; hold the low-drag attitude until near VX
Poor trim; roll in two turns of nose-up trim before takeoff
final_quiz.why: Premature rotation increases drag, decreases acceleration and lengthens the takeoff [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]; the roll should be in a low-drag attitude until VX approaches [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

final_quiz.q: In a retractable trainer, your learner plans to raise the gear the moment the wheels leave a short runway. What do you teach?
options: Raise it at once, since gear drag is the main thing that slows the climb
Wait for a positive rate of climb, then for obstacles cleared and VY
Leave it down until 1,000 feet AGL on every takeoff, whatever the runway
Raise it only after the flaps are fully up, so the trim change is small
final_quiz.why: Do not retract the gear until a positive rate of climb shows on the instruments [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]; on a short-field takeoff, gear and flaps stay in takeoff position until clear of obstacles and VY is established [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

final_quiz.q: The engine quits during the VX climb. Why does the nose have to come down at once?
options: VX is a low-power climb, so the engine has very little left to restart with
The VX climb keeps the airplane inside ground effect, which then ends abruptly
The flaps are always up in a VX climb, so the stall speed is higher than usual
VX is often just above stall speed; without power it is near the stall AOA
final_quiz.why: In a propeller airplane, maximum angle of climb is frequently just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]], and at a climb pitch attitude without power the airplane is at or near a stalling AOA, so lower the nose immediately [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: The RMH pilot's airplane needs 4,700 feet over 50 feet at 2,740 pounds; her personal margin is 20 percent; the runway is 5,000 feet. What did she decide?
options: Go, because 4,700 feet is less than the 5,000-foot runway
Wait at the strip for a headwind strong enough to fix the numbers
Cancel the trip and send her passengers home on the airline
Meet her passengers at a 9,200-foot runway and depart from there
final_quiz.why: With 20 percent, 4,700 feet becomes 5,640 feet, more than the runway [[30:36|RMH 4-3]]. She had the passengers go to the 9,200-foot runway [[30:41|RMH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Sample short-field table: 2,200 pounds, 5,000 feet, 30 °C, total 2,465 feet; 9-knot headwind; the strip is 2,500 feet with trees. Your learner says, 'With the wind it fits.' What do you point out?
options: Nothing; 2,218.5 feet fits inside a 2,500-foot strip with room
Headwinds don't change short-field chart numbers, so it's 2,465 feet
With wind it is 2,218.5 feet, but a 20% margin makes it about 2,662
Use only the ground roll, 1,305 feet, since the trees don't matter
final_quiz.why: 2,465 x 0.90 = 2,218.5 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. 2,218.5 x 1.20 = 2,662 feet, using a 20 percent margin like the RMH pilot's [[30:32|RMH 3-14]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's eyes are glued to the airspeed indicator in the VX climb and the pitch keeps oscillating. What is the error and fix?
options: Airspeed fixation; set the attitude outside, then glance at airspeed
Premature flap retraction; leave the flaps down to 1,000 feet AGL
Inadequate rotation; pull harder right at lift-off so the airplane slows to VX
Wheelbarrowing; add more back pressure during the takeoff roll
final_quiz.why: Fixation on the airspeed indicator is a listed short-field error [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]; airspeed lags attitude, so set the attitude, hold it and then check [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's short-field work is consistent at the home field's 6,000-foot runway. Per the AIH short-field example, what is a good next layer?
options: Repeat the same takeoff ten more times at the home field for consistency
Discuss a short obstructed strip, near max weight, high density altitude
Send the learner solo to a real short strip to apply the skill there
Move on to commercial maneuvers since the skill is now complete
final_quiz.why: The AIH adds those layers in discussion, with little extra ground time and no added flight time [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a simulated power loss right after a short-field lift-off. What must you settle beforehand?
options: Who has the throttle, and ending it once the outcome is clear
Which direction the learner will turn back toward the runway
Nothing at all, because surprise makes the training realistic
Who will talk to the tower while the learner handles the airplane
final_quiz.why: Either instructor or pilot has complete control of the throttle, and every simulated emergency approach ends once a safe outcome is or isn't assured [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Done wrong, simulated failures have caused accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says, 'Our chart is from a new airplane; ours is 30 years old with a tired engine.' What does the PHAK say?
options: Adjust the numbers when the airplane or pilot is below the chart's basis
Ignore it, because certification guarantees the published numbers
The charts already include a built-in margin for older airplanes and engines
Adjust only for altitude and temperature, never for airplane age
final_quiz.why: Chart data come from a new airplane with average piloting skill; compensate when the airplane or the pilot is below that [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

final_quiz.q: Departing a dark rural strip at night over trees, the learner feels the nose is too high right after lift-off and pushes forward. What is the likely cause?
options: Ground effect pitch-up as the airplane climbs out of it
Wake turbulence rolling and pitching the airplane
Carburetor ice reducing power just after lift-off
Somatogravic illusion from the takeoff acceleration
final_quiz.why: Rapid acceleration with poor visual references can give a false nose-up feeling, and the pilot may push the nose down [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: In the RMH turf-strip accident, what do the NTSB excerpts say the POH lacked?
options: Any takeoff distance data at all for the airplane model
Data for wet grass on turf or for a 100-foot obstacle
Published VX and VY speeds for the takeoff weight
A weight and balance section with passenger loading
final_quiz.why: The POH showed about 1,700 feet over 50 feet on a hard surface and had no data for wet grass or a 100-foot obstacle [[30:64|RMH C-1]].

takeaways: You hold the obstacle clearance speed or VX ±5 and VY ±5 while explaining; your private learner is held to +10/-5.
Every foot of runway, full power before brake release, low-drag roll, rotate at VX, VX to the obstacle or 50 feet, then VY.
VX is slow and close to the stall angle of attack: precision and an immediate nose-down after power loss.
Work the chart with the learner, read the conditions box and notes, then add a personal margin and say the decision aloud.
Name a realistic imaginary obstacle on the ground; do the teaching before the radio call.
Gear and flaps wait until clear and at VY; flaps come up in increments.
The best short-field decision is sometimes to leave the passengers on a longer runway.
cfi_notes: The AFH says holding the brakes to full rpm has not been shown to shorten the run in all light singles [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. The ACS asks for brakes while setting power and power confirmed before brake release (ACS AI.VII.E.S7, S8), and the sample chart assumes full throttle prior to brake release [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Teach the ACS and POH method, and explain the AFH remark when a learner asks.

The ACS lets you fly 'the recommended obstacle clearance airspeed or VX.' On the sample table that is the 'AT 50 ft' speed, 56 KIAS at 2,400 pounds [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Brief which number your airplane's POH uses before the flight so you and the examiner agree on the target.

The AFH normal-takeoff advice for gusty wind (extra speed before lift-off) [[24:137|AFH 6-5]] is silent for short fields, and extra speed lengthens the takeoff with the square of speed [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. Treat strong gusts on a short field as a go/no-go factor and use the POH guidance.

In the sample short-field table, the 2,000-pound rows in the 30 °C column at 5,000 to 7,000 feet show ground rolls larger than the total over 50 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Keep learner exercises off those cells.
The AIH short-field scenario example is written about landings [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. The same layering (short strip, obstruction, heavy, high density altitude) applies directly to takeoffs.

The AWH windshear studies describe large airplanes flown by crews [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. The pitch lesson carries over, but there is no light-single escape procedure in these sources; the PHAK points to AC 00-54 [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

Learners who come to you with a private-standard habit of flying VX 'a little fast for safety' need to hear why: lift-off speed and distance go together [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]], and in some airplanes 5 knots costs a lot of climb [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Examiners often test the go/no-go orally. Be ready to work Figure 11-24 by hand, apply the notes in order, and state a margin and a decision.
gaps: No source defines a 'safe maneuvering altitude' for S13. The AFH normal-takeoff advice to keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles [[24:137|AFH 6-5]] is a reasonable guide.
Beyond the AIH 'realistic point' [[25:192|AIH 10-8]] and the ACS 50 feet, no source says where or how high to place an imaginary obstacle.
No single-engine source gives a method or minimum altitude for simulating an engine failure during the VX climb; that is school SOP and instructor judgment.
These sources give no required takeoff safety factor for light airplanes; the 20 percent figure is one RMH pilot's personal minimum [[30:32|RMH 3-14]].
Real VX, VY, obstacle clearance speeds, flap settings and corrections for wet grass, slope or obstacles taller than 50 feet come only from the POH/AFM, and many POHs lack them [[30:64|RMH C-1]].

activities.title: Run the numbers with your learner
activities.intro: Use Figure 11-24 and the lesson's sources, then type your answer.

items.q: Figure 11-24, sea level, 0 °C: going from 2,000 to 2,200 pounds is 10 percent more weight. By what percent does the ground roll grow?
items.why: 525 to 650 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]: (650 - 525) / 525 x 100 = 23.8 percent, which matches the PHAK rule of at least 21 percent for 10 percent more weight [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: 2,000 pounds, 4,000 feet, 10 °C, with a 9-knot headwind. Corrected total distance to clear 50 feet?
items.why: Table total 1,500 feet; minus 10 percent for 9 knots of headwind: 1,500 x 0.90 = 1,350 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

items.q: 2,400 pounds, 1,000 feet, 30 °C, with a 4-knot tailwind. Corrected total distance to clear 50 feet?
items.why: Table total 2,000 feet; plus 10 percent per 2 knots of tailwind, so 20 percent: 2,000 x 1.20 = 2,400 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

items.q: RMH case: 3,600 feet over 50 feet at 2,500 pounds, plus her 20 percent margin. What runway length does she want?
items.why: 3,600 x 1.20 = 4,320 feet [[30:32|RMH 3-14]], which fits her 5,000-foot runway with 680 feet to spare [[30:36|RMH 4-3]].

items.q: PHAK example: the maximum rate profile climbs 1,500 feet while covering 6,000 feet over the ground. At a steady climb, how high is it after 3,000 feet over the ground, where the maximum angle profile is already at 1,000 feet?
items.why: 1,500 / 6,000 = 0.25 foot per foot; 0.25 x 3,000 = 750 feet [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. The angle profile is 250 feet higher at the same spot.

items.q: A trainer has a 36-foot wingspan. Below about what wing height is induced drag cut about 50 percent by ground effect?
items.why: About 50 percent at a height of 1/10 span: 36 / 10 = 3.6 feet [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

activities.title: True or false: risk on the climb-out
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A larger aircraft starts making wake vortices when it rotates.
cards.why: True. Vortices are generated from the moment it rotates until touchdown [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

cards.s: Departing behind a larger aircraft, rotate after its rotation point so you climb over its wake.
cards.why: False. Rotate prior to its rotation point and climb above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: Most stall/spin accidents come from intentional stall practice.
cards.why: False. Intentional practice seldom resulted in accidents; the danger was inadvertent stalls induced by distractions [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

cards.s: Until all obstacles are cleared, the AFH wants the pilot's focus outside, not on the gear or flap controls.
Tailwind and crosswind considerations take precedence over noise abatement in runway selection.
On a wet runway, an abort is no harder because brakes work the same on water.
cards.why: False. Hydroplaning tires give almost no braking or directional control [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

activities.title: First short-field lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner flies good normal takeoffs and today starts short-field work at a 4,500-foot runway with no obstacles. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On the ground, how do you set up the 'obstacle'?
options: Tell them to climb as steeply as they can, since the steepest angle always clears any obstacle
Name a 50-foot obstacle at a realistic landmark past the runway end, and the point to transition to VY
Skip it, since there are no trees, and have them just climb at VY to pattern altitude
Pick the hills 10 miles away and tell them to treat those as the obstacle for the climb
steps.why: Specify an imaginary obstacle at a realistic point [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; with no obstacle, VX to at least 50 feet, then VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

steps.s: Taxiing onto the runway, the learner asks how much back pressure to use at rotation. What now?
options: Give a full explanation now, since the learner asked and will not rotate correctly without it
Give a short cue now and save the detail for the debrief; the teaching belonged before the radio call
Ignore the question for now and say nothing about it afterward either, so he works out the pressure alone
Stop on the runway to explain the back pressure properly, then start the takeoff roll when he is ready
steps.why: Teaching while entering the runway takes attention from control and runway clearance; do most teaching before the tower or CTAF call [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: The learner turns onto the runway 400 feet past the threshold. What do you say?
options: 'Nothing; 4,100 feet is plenty for this airplane, so we can start from here'
'Short field means every foot: back-taxi to the very beginning'
'Do a rolling takeoff to make up for the lost 400 feet and keep the airplane moving'
'Use more flaps than normal to shorten the ground roll and make up for it'
steps.why: A short-field takeoff starts at the very beginning of the takeoff area [[24:143|AFH 6-11]], and not using all available runway is a listed error [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Habits built here go to the real strip.

steps.s: At 30 feet, still at VX, the learner reaches for the flap switch. What do you do?
options: Let them; flaps now improve the climb and give more margin over the obstacle
'Hands off, eyes outside: VX to 50, then VY, then flaps in steps'
Take the controls and land straight ahead on the remaining runway, then debrief
Tell them to raise the gear first, then the flaps, since the gear makes more drag
steps.why: Gear and flaps stay until clear of obstacles and VY is established; until then the pilot looks outside; flaps come up in increments [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

steps.s: In the debrief, every attempt crossed 50 feet about 8 knots fast. What is your fix for the next flight?
options: Accept it, since extra speed is a safety margin over the obstacle and nothing needs to change next flight
Teach a firmer rotation to the VX attitude, with more back pressure as the airplane accelerates
Rotate earlier, below the recommended rotation speed, so the airplane lifts off already at VX
Use less power at the start of the takeoff roll so the airplane accelerates more slowly
steps.why: That is inadequate rotation resulting in excessive speed after lift-off; the airplane accelerates after lift-off, so more back pressure holds a constant airspeed [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
